analysis.one_liner: Bans federal agencies from using facial recognition and biometric surveillance without new authorizing legislation.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or floor vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar any federal agency, employee, or contractor from acquiring or using facial recognition, gait recognition, or voice recognition surveillance systems anywhere in the United States — including airports, ports of entry, and border zones — unless Congress later passes a law specifically authorizing that use, with accuracy audits and privacy protections written in [S2][S3]. Information gathered in violation of the ban could not be used in federal court proceedings, individuals could sue for damages, and state attorneys general could sue on residents' behalf [S3]. It would also cut off federal Byrne law enforcement grants to state and local governments that use biometric surveillance without adopting comparable restrictions [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who would otherwise be subject to mass identification and tracking by government cameras and databases — including travelers, protesters, and residents of cities where police run facial recognition searches — gain a legal right against the technology and a way to sue if it is used against them [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary people subject to government biometric tracking

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits federal agencies, officials, and contractors from acquiring or using any facial recognition, gait, or voice recognition surveillance system in the U.S. unless Congress specifically authorizes it by name, with accuracy and privacy standards [S2][S3].

Makes information obtained through illegal biometric surveillance inadmissible in federal proceedings and gives aggrieved individuals the right to sue for actual and punitive damages, with state attorneys general able to sue on residents' behalf [S3].

Cuts federal Byrne public safety grants to state and local governments that use biometric surveillance without adopting substantially similar bans, and bars federal funds from being spent purchasing such systems [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal law enforcement and security agencies, and facial recognition vendors selling to them, lose access to a government market. Police departments that rely on facial recognition searches would lose federal grant money unless they adopt similar bans [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Police agencies and facial recognition vendors

drawbacks.text: Law enforcement groups argue facial recognition helps identify suspects, missing persons, and victims, and a full moratorium removes that tool even where accuracy audits and safeguards could address error rates [S2].

The bill defines 'biometric surveillance system' as any software performing real-time or recorded facial recognition, which would sweep in some uses that police say are narrowly targeted, such as identifying a specific suspect from a photo in a violent-crime investigation [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades a real law enforcement capability for a protection against mass surveillance, including the well-documented risk that facial recognition misidentifies people, with error rates higher for women and people with darker skin — which is why it requires accuracy audits by gender, skin color, and age before any use is authorized. The cost is genuine but targeted; the benefit is a legal check on a technology that can track anyone who walks past a camera.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate introduced the bill and referred it to the Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Markey introduced the bill on March 7, 2023, joined by Senators Merkley, Warren, Sanders, and Wyden [S1][S3].
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day [S5].
No further action was taken — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Police agencies and facial recognition vendors are better off because the bill died without a vote, leaving government use of the technology unrestricted by federal law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police agencies and biometric surveillance vendors

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to prohibit federal biometric surveillance without explicit statutory authorization and withhold Byrne grants from noncompliant state and local governments.

for.name: Sens. Merkley, Warren, Sanders, and Wyden
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; Sanders, an Independent, brought the total to 5 cosponsors, all from the progressive wing.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Dick Durbin (D-IL)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 7, 2023 and took no action — no hearing or markup — for the remaining 22 months of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 5 cosponsors were Democrats plus one Independent aligned with Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced past referral [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Facial recognition and biometric surveillance vendors
industries.note: The bill removes their government market — federal agencies could not buy or use their systems, and state and local police would face grant cuts unless they adopt similar bans [S2][S3]. Vendors' business depends on government contracts that this bill would cut off. Their gain from the bill's failure is the public's continued exposure to tracking.

industries.industry: Federal law enforcement and security agencies
industries.note: Agencies that use facial recognition for investigations, airport screening, and border identification would have to stop unless Congress authorizes specific uses with accuracy and privacy safeguards [S3].
Departments that use facial recognition would lose Byrne public safety grants unless they adopt comparable bans; departments without such systems are unaffected [S2][S3].
